name: In-group favouritism
statement: People give more to members of their own group than to outsiders, and a group invented minutes earlier is enough to produce it.
meaning: The claim has two halves and they are usually run together. The first is that group membership shifts how people allocate money and how far they cooperate. The second is that the membership can be arbitrary, with no shared history, no contact and no common interest. Tajfel's minimal group paradigm was built to isolate the second half by removing everything else, leaving a category label and nothing behind it. The measured quantity is favouritism rather than hostility. Balliet, Wu and De Dreu found that people cooperate more with ingroup members than with unclassified strangers, and treat outgroup members no differently from strangers. What moves is the ingroup being lifted, not the outgroup being pushed down.

origin.who: Henri Tajfel, Michael Billig, R. P. Bundy and Claude Flament
origin.note: The paper reports the first minimal group experiments and supplies the allocation matrices the paradigm still uses. Wiley serves it to no repository. Unpaywall recorded it as closed with no open location on 17 August 2026, and ResearchGate refused the request. The design and results described on this page are read instead from Tajfel's own account of the same experiments, published in Scientific American a year earlier.

evidence: Tajfel's first experiment used 64 boys aged 14 and 15 from a state, or comprehensive, school in a suburb of Bristol, tested in groups of eight. All eight in each group came from the same house and the same form, so they knew each other well before the experiment. They estimated the number of dots in 40 clusters flashed on a screen. Half were then told that people consistently over- or underestimate, half that people differ in accuracy, and the assignment to groups was random either way. Each boy worked alone in a cubicle through a booklet of six matrices, each printed three times, awarding points worth a tenth of a penny to two other boys known only by code number and group. The three printings paired two ingroup members, two outgroup members, or one of each. Nobody could award anything to himself, and each boy went home with about a dollar's worth. Choices were scored as ranks from 1 to 14, with 7.5 the fairness point. The intergroup choices favoured the ingroup, and both kinds of intragroup choice fell at 7.5. A second experiment tested three new groups of 16 boys, shown 12 unsigned reproductions, six by Klee and six by Kandinsky. Stated preference was the ostensible basis of the split and the assignment was random. Its matrices pulled maximum joint profit, maximum ingroup profit and maximum difference apart. Maximum joint profit, in Tajfel's words, exerted hardly any effect. The pull of maximum difference against joint profit and ingroup profit together was strong, so the boys gave up money for their own group in absolute terms to widen the gap. Tajfel reports of later experiments that discrimination rose rather than faded as the situation became familiar, and that most choices are a compromise between fairness and favouring one's own group.

replication.headline: Across 125 effect sizes people cooperate more with ingroup members at d = 0.32, and the effect falls to d = 0.04 when the partner does not know the participant's group.
replication.detail: Balliet, Wu and De Dreu searched PsycINFO and Google Scholar to September 2013 and found 77 articles containing 212 eligible studies, published between 1965 and 2013. Collapsing non-independent effect sizes left 125 for the ingroup-versus-outgroup contrast in cooperation, giving a random-effects d of 0.32, 95% CI [0.27, 0.38]. Heterogeneity was high, I-squared = 77.75, and the 90% prediction interval ran from -0.07 to 0.73, so the next study in this literature is not guaranteed to find anything. The condition that matters most is who knows what. Where both people know each other's group membership the effect is d = 0.32, 95% CI [0.27, 0.37]; where only the participant knows, it is d = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.12, 0.21], and the difference between the two is Q(1) = 10.08, p = .001. Interdependence moves it the same way: within minimal groups, dictator games give d = 0.19 and social dilemmas and trust games together give d = 0.39, 95% CI [0.30, 0.47], Q(1) = 4.06, p = .04. Whether the groups were real or invented in the laboratory made no reliable difference, d = 0.30 against d = 0.35, Q(1) = 0.84, p = .36. Cooperation with outgroup members was no different from cooperation with unclassified strangers, d = -0.09, 95% CI [-0.17, 0.00], which is the result that separates favouritism from derogation. Tom Lane's meta-analysis of economics experiments reaches a compatible figure from a different literature, and Lane reports his estimate as not distinguishable from Balliet's. Romano and colleagues ran the comparison on samples drawn to be representative for age, gender and income. Their trust games with 3,236 people across 17 societies found greater trust extended to ingroup members than to outgroup members and strangers, b = 0.19, p < 0.001. They report only a small amount of cross-societal variation, and no support for material security, religiosity or pathogen stress as explanations of it. Their reputation manipulation raised cooperation with ingroup and outgroup partners alike. Their preregistered prisoner's dilemma across 42 nations, with 18,411 people recruited, found national parochialism at d = 0.22 overall, reaching statistical significance in 39 of the 42 nations, b = 0.29, p < 0.001. Two studies set the minimal group inductions against each other. Pinter and Greenwald tested four and found comparable favouritism on explicit measures of attraction and identification and on bonus money allocation, with a memorisation procedure largest on implicit measures. Schmidt and Drake tested six and report in their abstract that participants favoured their minimal ingroup on most outcome measures whatever the procedure, with the size varying by outcome, induction and method.

study.cite: Balliet, D., Wu, J., & De Dreu, C. K. W. (2014). Ingroup favoritism in cooperation: A meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1556-1581.

replicated.weighting: random effects, non-independent effect sizes collapsed

limits: The two literatures measure different things and the meta-analysis says so. Balliet and colleagues excluded Tajfel-style matrix studies on the grounds that they are not comparable with the games and carry no variation in interdependence, reciprocity or reputation. So the pooled 0.32 is not a replication of Tajfel, and no standardised effect size for the 1971 experiments was located in either Tajfel source read here, which is why no original figure appears above. Their own dictator-game figure does not settle: the text reports d = 0.19, 95% CI [0.07, 0.37], Table 7 reports [0.01, 0.36] for minimal groups and [0.08, 0.32] with natural groups added, and Table 6 prints 0.15. The interval in the text matches neither table, so 0.19 is quoted here without one. Romano's 18,411 is the number recruited; the main analysis dropped participants who failed an attention check, the analysed count is not given in the article, and the authors report the results unchanged with everyone included. The matrices themselves measure relative differentiation rather than plain generosity, and Deschrijver and Ramsey's seven preregistered experiments found the same allocation strategies against a single other person who merely differed, with no groups and no identities in play. Kerr, Ao, Hogg and Zhang began an adversarial collaboration because a series of studies had failed to replicate minimal group favouritism, and located moderators including social isolation, mode of instruction and country. Their article is paywalled at Elsevier and is described here only from its abstract as recorded at Semantic Scholar. Lane's published article is open access under CC BY at Elsevier, and every request for it from here was refused. Its abstract gives 441 results from 77 studies where the 2015 CeDEx discussion paper gives 447. The Lane figures on this page are the discussion paper's and may not be the published ones. That paper is also inconsistent with itself on how many of the 447 carry an effect size, giving 368 in the method and 364 in the results. Schmidt and Drake's article is listed as gold open access at the University of California Press, whose server refused these requests. Their Open Science Framework project holds preregistrations, materials and data but not the article, so it is described only from its abstract at Crossref. Perry's book was not read; her archival findings are quoted from her own 2014 article in The Psychologist. Searches on 17 August 2026 covered Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, PubMed Central, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, the Open Science Framework, Frontiers, the Classics in the History of Psychology text of Sherif's monograph, a hosted copy of Scientific American, and web search.
misreadings: Robbers Cave is the study usually produced as the demonstration, and it demonstrates something else. Sherif and colleagues put boys through weeks of engineered competition at a summer camp, which is the opposite of a minimal group, and Tajfel drew the contrast himself: Sherif's groups had to be placed in intense competition for several days, where a dot-estimation label was enough. The camp study is also retold as a clean natural history of conflict. Sherif's own monograph records that 1954 was not the first attempt and that a 1953 study was 'terminated as an experiment owing to various difficulties and unfavorable conditions, including errors of judgment in the direction of the experiment'. Gina Perry worked through Sherif's archive and traced surviving participants. At the 1953 camp at Middle Grove, she reports, the boys who had made friends in the opening whole-group phase resented being separated from them, both teams accused staff of bias and favouritism, and one boy found a staff notebook of observations. She reports that inflating one team's scores to raise rivalry was common in both 1953 and 1954, and that staff at the 1953 camp pulled a tent down hoping one group would blame the other. A second misreading treats arbitrary groups as a floor, on the assumption that race or nationality must move people further than a painting preference. In Lane's working paper the artificial identities average d = 0.353, 95% CI [0.266, 0.439], against ethnicity at d = 0.134, 95% CI [0.013, 0.255], with gender running the other way at d = -0.177, 95% CI [-0.301, -0.053]. Arbitrary is not the ceiling either: social and geographic groupings top his table at d = 0.551, 95% CI [0.432, 0.669]. A third reading treats the effect as hostility toward outsiders. Everett, Faber and Crockett conclude that favouritism is driven by both preferences and beliefs, and that Balliet's meta-analysis points to the stronger role for beliefs, meaning expectations about what the other person will do. Two neighbouring entries carry claims that are related without being this one. The out-group homogeneity effect is a judgement about how varied a group looks, and out-group favouritism is the reversal found in low-status groups.

sources.text: Tajfel, H., Billig, M. G., Bundy, R. P., & Flament, C. (1971). Social categorization and intergroup behaviour. European Journal of Social Psychology, 1(2), 149-178. Closed at Wiley with no open location at Unpaywall on 17 August 2026; named as the origin, and no figure on this page is taken from it.

Tajfel, H. (1970). Experiments in intergroup discrimination. Scientific American, 223(5), 96-102. Tajfel's own account of the same experiments; the design and results in this entry were read from a hosted copy of this article.

Balliet, D., Wu, J., & De Dreu, C. K. W. (2014). Ingroup favoritism in cooperation: A meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1556-1581. Full text read from the authors' hosted copy of the advance online version, linked here because the publisher's copy is paywalled.

Lane, T. (2016). Discrimination in the laboratory: A meta-analysis of economics experiments. European Economic Review, 90, 375-402. Open access under CC BY at Elsevier, whose server refused these requests; its abstract reports 441 results from 77 studies against the discussion paper's 447.

Lane, T. (2015). Discrimination in the laboratory: a meta-analysis. CeDEx Discussion Paper 2015-03, University of Nottingham. The version read for this entry; it reports 447 results from 77 studies and an overall effect size of 0.252, 95% CI [0.205, 0.300], from the sub-sample of observations carrying an effect size.

Romano, A., Balliet, D., Yamagishi, T., & Liu, J. H. (2017). Parochial trust and cooperation across 17 societies. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 114(48), 12702-12707. Read from the Europe PMC full text of the PubMed Central copy.

Romano, A., Sutter, M., Liu, J. H., Yamagishi, T., & Balliet, D. (2021). National parochialism is ubiquitous across 42 nations around the world. Nature Communications, 12, 4456. Read in full from the publisher's PDF; the source of the 18,411 recruited, the d of 0.22 and the 39 of 42 nations.

Schmidt, K., & Drake, R. G. (2023). Minimal group procedures and outcomes. Collabra: Psychology, 9(1), 90187. Gold open access, but the publisher's server refused these requests; described here from its abstract at Crossref.

Pinter, B., & Greenwald, A. G. (2011). A comparison of minimal group induction procedures. Group Processes & Intergroup Relations, 14(1), 81-98. Read from the authors' hosted final draft; all four inductions produced comparable ingroup favouritism on explicit measures and bonus money allocation.

Deschrijver, E., & Ramsey, R. (2025). Unequal resource division occurs in the absence of group division and identity. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 122(7), e2413797122. Seven preregistered experiments with more than 1,400 subjects, of which three used 238 UK participants each; read from the Europe PMC full text.

Paywalled at Elsevier and at Scopus; the description on this page comes from the abstract as recorded at Semantic Scholar, and no figure is taken from it.

Perry, G. (2018). The Lost Boys: Inside Muzafer Sherif's Robbers Cave Experiment. London: Scribe. The book-length account of the archival work; not read for this entry, and nothing here is quoted from it.
